label: History
value: Mr. Allan brought his young bride to Avonlea five years before the current time.
unit: Having brought his young bride to Avonlea five years prior, Mr. Allan served as the town's minister. During a social visit to Green Gables early in his tenure, he and his wife attended a tea prepared by Anne, where Mrs. Allan accidentally sampled a layer cake flavored with anodyne liniment. Following the sudden death of Matthew Cuthbert, Mr. Allan provided spiritual support and comfort to Anne as she grieved. His eventual departure from Avonlea was noted by the local community as Anne completed her tenure as the town's schoolteacher.

label: Personality
value: Anne Shirley is imaginative.
unit: Anne Shirley is an imaginative and highly talkative individual who is also known to be generous, though at times she can be careless and reckless. Her vivid imagination allows her to find optimism even in bad situations, though she sometimes catches herself acting without reflection. Driven by strong desires, she wants to remain at Green Gables, grow up to be good-looking, and work toward becoming a teacher like Miss Stacy, while at one point preferring to be called Cordelia. She demonstrates accountability by confessing her mistakes to take responsibility, such as when she resolved to confess a fault in order to attend a picnic.

label: History
value: Anne Shirley was raised as an adopted orphan without kith or kin.
unit: Raised as an adopted orphan without kith or kin, fourteen-year-old Anne Shirley arrived in Avonlea by mistake instead of the requested boy, but Marilla and Matthew Cuthbert decided to keep her at Green Gables. During her early years, she vowed eternal friendship with Diana Barry in the garden at Orchard Slope and once bought dye from a peddler that turned her red hair green, forcing Marilla to cut it off. Though she initially left school after being punished beside Gilbert Blythe, she eventually returned under Miss Stacy's mentorship, earning her teaching certificate at Queen's Academy and staying home to manage Green Gables when Matthew died and Marilla's sight failed. Anne taught at Avonlea and organized the Village Improvement Society—enduring misadventures like selling Mr. Harrison's cow by mistake—before heading to Redmond College with her friends. Early in her college years, she rejected a marriage proposal from Billy Andrews via his sister Jane, followed by a rejected proposal from Gilbert Blythe, which fractured their close dynamic. While pursuing her studies, Anne successfully wrote short pieces for publication and spent two years courted by Roy Gardner, whom she ultimately turned down upon realizing she did not love him. Learning that Gilbert was near death from typhoid fever forced Anne to acknowledge her true feelings, leading to their reconciliation and engagement after his recovery. After graduating, Anne took a teaching position at Valley Road for two years, and she later gathered with Diana at Green Gables to discuss her upcoming marriage to Gilbert and their planned move to Four Winds Harbor. Years later, after returning from a trip to Europe, Anne sat on the veranda at Ingleside with Susan Baker while her youngest children played nearby.

label: Quote
value: Anne Shirley said: "I’ll fold them nicely tonight. They always made us do that at the asylum. Half the time, though, I’d forget, I’d be in such a hurry to get into bed nice and quiet and imagine things."

label: Quote
value: Anne Shirley said: "I’d do anything to oblige you. But you’ll have to tell me what to say for this once. After I get into bed I’ll imagine out a real nice prayer to say always. I believe that it will be quite interesting, now that I come to think of it."

label: Quote
value: Anne Shirley said: "But I’d be ever so much gratefuller if—if you’d made just one of them with puffed sleeves. Puffed sleeves are so fashionable now. It would give me such a thrill, Marilla, just to wear a dress with puffed sleeves."

label: Quote
value: Anne Shirley said: "Oh, Marilla, I’m frightened—now that it has come I’m actually frightened. What if she shouldn’t like me! It would be the most tragical disappointment of my life."

label: Quote
value: Anne Shirley said: "I’ll just eat one tonight, Marilla. And I can give Diana half of them, can’t I? The other half will taste twice as sweet to me if I give some to her. It’s delightful to think I have something to give her."

label: History
value: Anne grew up as an unloved orphan girl
unit: Anne grew up as an unloved orphan girl, moving between homes and working as a drudge until Matthew and Marilla Cuthbert adopted her from an asylum and brought her to Green Gables in Avonlea. Early on, she faced near-expulsion from the home after falsely confessing to taking Marilla's brooch to attend a picnic, and she temporarily quit school after smashing a slate over Gilbert Blythe's head when he called her 'Carrots.' Her trajectory shifted when she saved the life of Diana Barry's sister, earning back her best friend, and later tied with Gilbert for first place on the Island during the Queen's Academy entrance examinations. After Matthew passed away, Anne gave up her college scholarship to remain in Avonlea to teach school, raise Marilla's orphaned distant twin relatives, Davy and Dora, and co-found the Avonlea Village Improvement Society. After eventually pursuing higher education at Redmond College, she rejected a rich suitor, Royal Gardner, realizing her true feelings lay with Gilbert, whom she accepted after he recovered from typhoid fever. The couple married at Green Gables and moved to Four Winds Harbor, where Anne survived the tragic death of her firstborn infant, Joyce, before giving birth to a healthy son, James Matthew. Overcoming her grief, she formed deep bonds with her neighbors, including Leslie Moore and Captain Jim, whose life story she helped inspire into a published book before his peaceful passing. The family subsequently relocated to Ingleside in Glen St. Mary, where Anne successfully raised six children while offering guidance to the town and defending the lively children of the local minister, Mr. Meredith.

Early on, she faced near-expulsion from the home after falsely confessing to taking Marilla's brooch to attend a picnic, and she temporarily quit school after smashing a slate over Gilbert Blythe's head when he called her 'Carrots.' Her trajectory shifted when she saved the life of Diana Barry's sister, earning back her best friend, and later tied with Gilbert for first place on the Island during the Queen's Academy entrance examinations. After Matthew passed away, Anne gave up her college scholarship to remain in Avonlea to teach school, raise Marilla's orphaned distant twin relatives, Davy and Dora, and co-found the Avonlea Village Improvement Society. After eventually pursuing higher education at Redmond College, she rejected a rich suitor, Royal Gardner, realizing her true feelings lay with Gilbert, whom she accepted after he recovered from typhoid fever. The couple married at Green Gables and moved to Four Winds Harbor, where Anne survived the tragic death of her firstborn infant, Joyce, before giving birth to a healthy son, James Matthew. Overcoming her grief, she formed deep bonds with her neighbors, including Leslie Moore and Captain Jim, whose life story she helped inspire into a published book before his peaceful passing. The family subsequently relocated to Ingleside in Glen St. Mary, where Anne successfully raised six children while offering guidance to the town and defending the lively children of the local minister, Mr. Meredith.

label: Quote
value: Anne said: "Well, that is another hope gone. ‘My life is a perfect graveyard of buried hopes.’ That’s a sentence I read in a book once, and I say it over to comfort myself whenever I’m disappointed in anything."

label: Quote
value: Anne said: “Oh, what I know about myself isn’t really worth telling,” said Anne eagerly. “If you’ll only let me tell you what I imagine about myself you’ll think it ever so much more interesting.”

label: Quote
value: Anne said: “I was afraid it might be Mrs. Spencer’s place,” said Anne mournfully. “I don’t want to get there. Somehow, it will seem like the end of everything.”

label: Quote
value: Anne said: “I—I saw it this afternoon when you were away at the Aid Society,” said Anne, a little slowly. “I was passing your door when I saw it on the cushion, so I went in to look at it.”

label: Quote
value: Anne said: “I did put it back,” said Anne quickly—pertly, Marilla thought. “I don’t just remember whether I stuck it on the pincushion or laid it in the china tray. But I’m perfectly certain I put it back.”

label: History
value: Aunt Jamesina came to live at Patty's Place
unit: Aunt Jamesina came to live at Patty's Place to act as housekeeper for Stella Maynard, Anne Shirley, and Priscilla Grant during their college years. She brought her two cats, Joseph and the Sarah-cat, and quickly established a comfortable, cheerful household routine with the girls, freely sharing her relaxed views on chaperoning and stories about her past suitors. Throughout their time together, she provided a warm domestic presence, chatting with the young women about their studies, romantic entanglements, and visitors, while witnessing major events such as Phil Gordon's engagement and Anne's suitors. Following the end of their college years and the group's departure from Patty's Place, Aunt Jamesina traveled to India to explore her daughter's mission field, overcoming her personal horror of snakes to do so.

Following the end of their college years and the group's departure from Patty's Place, Aunt Jamesina traveled to India to explore her daughter's mission field, overcoming her personal horror of snakes to do so.

label: Quote
value: Aunt Jamesina said: "She couldn’t take Joseph with her so she begged me to take him. I really couldn’t refuse. He’s a beautiful cat—that is, his disposition is beautiful. She called him Joseph because his coat is of many colors."

label: Quote
value: Aunt Jamesina said: "Kittens have to be drowned, I admit, or the world would be overrun. But no decent, grown-up cat should be done to death—unless he sucks eggs."

label: Quote
value: Aunt Jamesina said: "Well, I hope so, Anne. I do hope so, because I love her. But I can’t understand her—she beats me. She isn’t like any of the girls I ever knew, or any of the girls I was myself."

label: Quote
value: Aunt Jamesina said: "Yes, in my soul. But I’ll admit my legs aren’t as young as yours. You go and get some fresh air, Anne. You look pale lately."

label: Quote
value: Aunt Jamesina said: "Anybody is liable to rheumatism in her legs, Anne. It’s only old people who should have rheumatism in their souls, though. Thank goodness, I never have. When you get rheumatism in your soul you might as well go and pick out your coffin."

label: History
value: Aunt Josephine is the great-aunt of Diana Barry.
unit: Aunt Josephine was the wealthy great-aunt of Diana Barry who lived at Beechwood in Charlottetown. During a visit to Orchard Slope, she was infuriated when Anne Shirley and Diana accidentally jumped on top of her in the spare-room bed, but she was so won over by Anne's brave, sincere apology that she decided to stay in Avonlea and became firm friends with her. She later sent Anne kid slippers for Christmas and hosted Anne and Diana at her estate for the Exhibition in Charlottetown. After enduring a dreadful illness that lasted over a year, Aunt Josephine passed away, leaving Anne a legacy of one thousand dollars in her will to secure her college education.

label: Quote
value: Aunt Josephine said: “I’m afraid my imagination is a little rusty—it’s so long since I used it,” she said. “I dare say your claim to sympathy is just as strong as mine. It all depends on the way we look at it. Sit down here and tell me about yourself.”

label: Quote
value: Aunt Josephine said: “I’ve made up my mind to stay simply for the sake of getting better acquainted with that Anne-girl,” she said frankly. “She amuses me, and at my time of life an amusing person is a rarity.”

label: Quote
value: Aunt Josephine said: "Mercy, child, how you have grown! You’re taller than I am, I declare. And you’re ever so much better-looking than you used to be, too. But I dare say you know that without being told."

label: Quote
value: Aunt Josephine said: "Remember, you Anne-girl, when you come to town you’re to visit me and I’ll put you in my very sparest spare-room bed to sleep."

label: Quote
value: Aunt Josephine said: "Oh, I must, hey? I rather think Diana did her share of the jumping at least. Such carryings on in a respectable house!"

label: History
value: Aunt Martha is a cousin of John Meredith's mother
unit: Aunt Martha, a cousin of John Meredith's mother, was taken into the manse by Mr. Meredith to save her from going to the poorhouse. When runaway Mary Vance came to stay at the manse, Aunt Martha clashed slightly with her over the cooking while Mary assisted with house chores. Later, Aunt Martha fell bedridden with an illness, leaving Faith and Una to manage the household and care for a sick Carl until her recovery. She eventually caused an uproar with Faith when she killed Faith's pet rooster, Adam, to serve as dinner for a visiting minister, Mr. Perry.

label: History
value: Carl moves from Maywater
unit: Carl moves from Maywater to Glen St. Mary with his motherless siblings and minister father, settling into the manse and quickly forming a close bond with the local Blythe children in Rainbow Valley. Along with his brothers and sisters, he takes in a runaway orphan named Mary Vance, hiding her in their garret until she is eventually adopted by Miss Cornelia. Later, while his father is away and his aunt is sick, Carl falls ill himself while his sisters struggle to manage the household. To prevent further trouble and protect their father's reputation, Carl and his siblings form a self-policing Good-Conduct Club, through which they enforce strict rules and punishments on themselves. When the club's members decide to self-punish by holding a day-long fast, his sister Una faints from hunger at church, prompting their father to realize he needs to pay closer attention to raising them. Sometime later, after Carl is frightened by a fake ghost, his brother Jerry punishes his cowardice by ordering him to sit in the cold, rainy graveyard until midnight. This ordeal causes Carl to contract double pneumonia and face a grim fight for his life, though he ultimately recovers to the community's relief. Carl eventually incurs his father's wrath after pulling a prank with an eel on a local woman, though his father finds himself unable to whip him upon looking into his eyes. In the end, after Una selflessly asks Rosemary West to marry their father, Carl's family prepares for his father's upcoming wedding while celebrating with their friends in Rainbow Valley.

label: History
value: Charlotta the Fourth was a young maid.
unit: Charlotta the Fourth was a young maid who worked for Miss Lavendar Lewis at Echo Lodge when she was fourteen years old. She often entertained visiting guests alongside her employer, hosting pretend tea parties in the garden. Concerned by Miss Lavendar's frequent melancholy, Charlotta confided her worries to Anne Shirley, leading Anne to promise to visit more often. She later helped Anne prepare the house for Stephen Irving's return, anxiously waiting in the kitchen until she witnessed the couple's happy reconciliation. Charlotta subsequently assisted with the wedding preparations at Echo Lodge, eventually marrying a good-tempered bricklayer named Tom. Years later, she traveled back to Avonlea to attend Anne's wedding to Gilbert Blythe at Green Gables.

label: Quote
value: Charlotta said: "it’s plain to be seen you and Miss Lavendar have got a secret and I think, begging your pardon if I’m too forward, Miss Shirley, ma’am, that it’s real mean not to tell me when we’ve all been such chums."

label: Quote
value: Charlotta said: "I peeked from the kitchen window . . . and he’s awful handsome . . . and just the right age for Miss Lavendar. And oh, Miss Shirley, ma’am, do you think it would be much harm to listen at the door?"

label: Quote
value: Charlotta said: "But I’m sure I shan’t sleep a blessed wink, Miss Shirley, ma’am, for fear that something’ll go wrong at the last minute . . . the cream won’t whip . . . or Mr. Irving’ll have a stroke and not be able to come."

label: Quote
value: Charlotta said: "but there’s so much to do yet . . . and oh, Miss Shirley, ma’am, I’m skeered it’s going to rain and I wish you’d get up and tell me you think it ain’t."

label: Quote
value: Charlotta said: "Yes, ma’am. Come in, ma’am. I’ll tell Miss Lavendar you’re here, ma’am. She’s upstairs, ma’am."

value: Cornelia Bryant is known for her bitter tongue.

Despite her sharp demeanor and a tendency to be considered cracked on the subject of Methodists, she privately acknowledges herself to be a lonely soul who prefers to avoid useless arguments and enjoys reading obituary notices for recreation. Extremely neat in her habits, she is an exceptionally talented cook who frequently prepares nice food for others, having even won a prize for her lemon pies. Additionally, she takes quiet pride in her abilities as the best sewer in the local area, skilled in both sewing and hand embroidery.

However, after Anne passionately defended the minister's family, Cornelia shifted her stance to champion the children's unique strengths, eventually joining her friends in celebrating the upcoming double wedding of the minister and his bride.

value: Cornelia Bryant said: "You always look as cool as a cucumber, Anne, dearie. Do I smell cherry pie? If I do, ask me to stay to tea. Haven’t tasted a cherry pie this summer. My cherries have all been stolen by those scamps of Gilman boys from the Glen."

label: Quote
value: Cornelia Bryant said: "There’s a great change come over her lately. She laughs and jokes like a girl, and from her talk I gather she’s here real often."

label: Quote
value: Cornelia Bryant said: "Now, you needn’t Miss Cornelia me, Anne, dearie. ANYBODY would have thought the same. If the Montreal doctors can make a rational creature out of Dick Moore they’re wonders."

label: Quote
value: Cornelia Bryant said: "Yes. They run up just like the steps of a stair. Gerald’s the oldest. He’s twelve and they call him Jerry. He’s a clever boy. Faith is eleven. She is a regular tomboy but pretty as a picture, I must say."

During his early months at Green Gables, Davy frequently caused chaos by dropping a caterpillar down a girl's neck at church, putting a toad in Marilla's bed, ruining Dora's dress, and locking his sister in a toolhouse. He repeatedly struggled with lying and skipping his prayers, but Anne consistently counseled him through his confessions and guilt. Despite misbehaving further by spoiling dinner party pies during a visit from a famous author, Davy retained a permanent home at Green Gables after money from his late father's brother provided for the twins' upkeep. Over the years, Davy grew attached to Anne, confiding his jealousies, theological confusions, and moral dilemmas to her, including a night when he confessed to skipping Sunday School to go fishing. As Anne attended college, Davy welcomed her back during her holiday visits, sharing chatter about his schoolwork, lost teeth, and childhood musings. He was present with his family when Anne married Gilbert Blythe in the Green Gables orchard, and he later traveled from Avonlea to spend Christmas with the newly married couple at their home in Four Winds.

Despite misbehaving further by spoiling dinner party pies during a visit from a famous author, Davy retained a permanent home at Green Gables after money from his late father's brother provided for the twins' upkeep. Over the years, Davy grew attached to Anne, confiding his jealousies, theological confusions, and moral dilemmas to her, including a night when he confessed to skipping Sunday School to go fishing. As Anne attended college, Davy welcomed her back during her holiday visits, sharing chatter about his schoolwork, lost teeth, and childhood musings. He was present with his family when Anne married Gilbert Blythe in the Green Gables orchard, and he later traveled from Avonlea to spend Christmas with the newly married couple at their home in Four Winds.

label: Quote
value: Davy Keith said: "I just did it for fun. Things have been so awful quiet here for so long that I thought it would be fun to give you folks a big scare. It was, too."

label: Quote
value: Davy Keith said: “I never will, now that I know it’s bad,” asseverated Davy between sobs. “If you ever catch me telling a whopper again you can . . .” Davy groped mentally for a suitable penance . . . “you can skin me alive, Anne.”

label: Quote
value: Davy Keith said: “Why?” queried Davy, settling comfortably down and looking up with a tearstained, investigating face. “Why ain’t whopper as good as falsehood? I want to know. It’s just as big a word.”

label: Quote
value: Davy Keith said: “Then,” said Davy decidedly, “Marilla is bad, for she tells them. And she’s worse’n me, for I didn’t know it was wrong but she does.”

label: Quote
value: Davy Keith said: “I’ll do it,” volunteered Davy, “if Marilla’ll hold them by the legs, ’cause I guess it’d take both my hands to manage the axe. It’s awful jolly fun to see them hopping about after their heads are cut off.”

label: History
value: Di grew up as part of the Blythe family at Ingleside.
unit: Di grew up as part of the Blythe family at Ingleside, forming an exceptionally close bond with her brother Walter, who shared his original poetry exclusively with her. She spent much of her childhood playing with her siblings and the neighboring Meredith children in their favorite spot, Rainbow Valley, where they shared meals, stories, and dreams for the future. When Mary Vance criticized Faith Meredith for a church scandal, Di and her sister Nan loyally defended Faith. Di continued to spend her evenings gathered in Rainbow Valley with the other children, listening to Walter share myths and poetry, discussing local ghost stories, and hearing about everyone's aspirations. She was also present in the valley to celebrate her brother Jem's final evening with the group before he left for Queen's Academy.

label: History
value: Diana was named by a schoolmaster who boarded at her home when she was born.
unit: Diana was named by a schoolmaster who boarded at her home when she was born, and as a girl in Avonlea, she learned fancy crochet stitches from her aunt in Carmody, imagined ghosts in the Haunted Wood with Anne Shirley, helped form a schoolgirl story club, and swore a solemn oath of eternal friendship with Anne in the garden at Orchard Slope. During their schooldays, Diana accidentally became intoxicated at Green Gables after drinking currant wine that Anne mistook for raspberry cordial, leading Mrs. Barry to temporarily forbid the girls from playing together. Their friendship was restored after Anne heroically saved Diana's sister Minnie May from croup while their parents were away. Diana and Anne later accidentally jumped onto Aunt Josephine Barry in a spare-room bed during a sleepover, but Anne managed to appease the angry aunt, securing Diana's continued music lessons. Diana later received a pair of kid slippers from Aunt Josephine for Christmas, helped launch the Village Improvement Society, and went on a festive trip to Charlottetown with Anne. When Anne took the Queen's Entrance exams, Diana brought the published results to Green Gables to announce Anne's first-place tie, and she later attended Redmond College news while remaining in Avonlea. Along with Jane Andrews, Diana unsuccessfully attempted to persuade Judson Parker to remove patent medicine ads from his fences, and she later accidentally got lost in the woods with Anne, leading them to meet Miss Lavendar Lewis at Echo Lodge. Diana became engaged to Fred Wright, and prior to her wedding, she secretly edited and submitted Anne's rejected manuscript to a baking powder contest, winning a prize for her friend. Following her wedding to Fred, Diana settled into married life as a matron and eventually welcomed a baby, continuing her lifelong, unshakeable bond with Anne through all of life's transitions.

label: Quote
value: Diana said: “Yes,” said Diana, tossing her head, “but I’m sure he doesn’t like Julia Bell so very much. I’ve heard him say he studied the multiplication table by her freckles.”

label: Quote
value: Diana said: “Those Pye girls are cheats all round,” said Diana indignantly, as they climbed the fence of the main road. “Gertie Pye actually went and put her milk bottle in my place in the brook yesterday. Did you ever? I don’t speak to her now.”

label: Quote
value: Diana said: "Why, he makes fun of all the girls. He laughs at mine because it’s so black. He’s called me a crow a dozen times; and I never heard him apologize for anything before, either."

label: Quote
value: Diana said: "I do think you’re mean. What shall I do? Mr. Phillips will make me sit with that horrid Gertie Pye—I know he will because she is sitting alone. Do come back, Anne."

label: Quote
value: Diana said: “The nicest I ever drank,” said Diana. “It’s ever so much nicer than Mrs. Lynde’s, although she brags of hers so much. It doesn’t taste a bit like hers.”

value: Dick Moore is a man.
unit: Dick Moore was a man living in Four Winds Harbor in a tragic situation, cared for by his wife Leslie while lacking his memory and sanity. After Captain Jim helped lead Dick home one fog-filled evening, Dr. Gilbert Blythe eventually came to believe that an operation on his skull might restore his faculties. Gilbert, Captain Jim, and Leslie decided to pursue the procedure in Montreal, borrowing money to pay for it. The operation was successful, but it restored the man's memory only to reveal that he was actually Dick's cousin, George Moore, and that the real Dick Moore had died years prior in Cuba.

value: Dora Keith was brought to live at Green Gables by Marilla Cuthbert.
unit: Dora Keith, along with her twin brother Davy, was brought to live at Green Gables by Marilla Cuthbert after their mother passed away. Early in her stay, Davy forced her to walk a pigpen fence and pumped water over her, ruining her dress. She was later locked in Mr. Harrison's toolhouse by her brother before being found by Anne Shirley and Mr. Barry. Following the death of her uncle Richard Keith, a trust fund was left that allowed Dora and Davy to stay permanently at Green Gables. As she grew older, Dora was comforted by Anne at school after being frightened by ghost stories. She later gave in to Davy's persuasion to skip Sunday School to go fishing, though Davy eventually confessed the trickery.

label: History
value: Ellen West resided at her home with her sister, Rosemary.
unit: Ellen West resided at her home with her sister, Rosemary, where she engaged John Meredith in discussions regarding European politics and German militarism during his visits. Holding Rosemary to a solemn vow they had made over their mother's Bible ten years prior never to marry, Ellen strictly warned her sister against romantic involvement with the widowed minister. When John proposed to Rosemary, Ellen adamantly refused to release her sister from the promise despite Rosemary's pleas, leading Rosemary to send him a rejection. Later, after Norman Douglas asked Rosemary to release Ellen from her vow so they could marry, Rosemary freed Ellen from her promise. However, Ellen declared she would still not marry Norman if it meant leaving Rosemary to live alone on the hill.

label: Quote
value: Ellen West said: "When you howl you’re hit, I’ve always heard, George. But she promised, Saint—she promised, and we Wests always keep our word. So it won’t matter if he does want to philander, George. She promised. I won’t worry."

label: Quote
value: Ellen West said: "It is not nonsense. It is my firm decision. It would be absurd for you to think of living here by yourself—a mile from any other house. If you won’t come with me I’ll stay with you. Now, we won’t argue the matter, so don’t try."

label: Quote
value: Ellen West said: "I will not do it. A promise is a promise in my eyes. I will not do it. Break your promise—be forsworn if you will—but it shall not be with any assent of mine."

label: Quote
value: Ellen West said: “I think it is just as well to be interested in things as long as you live,” she had said. “If you’re not, it doesn’t seem to me that there’s much difference between the quick and the dead.”

label: Quote
value: Ellen West said: “I won’t have you always,” Ellen had said, breaking her silence with harsh intensity. “You will marry and leave me. I shall be left all alone. I cannot bear the thought—I cannot. I would rather die.”

label: History
value: Faith moved from Maywater
unit: Faith moved from Maywater to Glen St. Mary with her widowed father, Mr. Meredith, and her siblings. Early on, she and her brothers and sister befriended the neighboring Blythe children in Rainbow Valley and sheltered a runaway orphan, Mary Vance, in their garret before Mary was adopted by a local woman. Faith frequently took impulsive actions to protect her family; after accidentally causing a scandal by cleaning house on a Sunday due to a mix-up in days, she publicly addressed the church congregation to clear her father's name. Soon after, upon learning that the church might lose crucial financial support, Faith boldly confronted the gruff Norman Douglas, ultimately securing his church attendance and salary contributions. When a visiting minister ate her cherished pet rooster, Adam, for dinner, Faith stood by in silent revenge as the man's coat-tails caught fire at the hearth, though she was later comforted over the bird's loss by Rosemary West.

label: History
value: Faith and her siblings formed a self-policing Good-Conduct Club.
unit: Following a string of missteps, Faith and her siblings formed a self-policing Good-Conduct Club. When Faith gave away her good stockings and faced wearing ugly striped ones to church, she attempted to make herself sick by standing on an ice bank in the graveyard; when that failed, she went to service bare-legged, leading to widespread local gossip that she ultimately addressed by publishing an explanatory letter in the town paper. During a later club-mandated fast to punish themselves for another disruption, her sister Una fainted at church, sparking public criticism of their upbringing. Despite these misadventures, Faith and her siblings continued playing in Rainbow Valley, once mistaking a neighbor in the dark for a ghost and fleeing in panic. She eventually celebrated the news of her father's upcoming wedding to Rosemary West alongside her family.

unit: Following a string of missteps, Faith and her siblings formed a self-policing Good-Conduct Club. When Faith gave away her good stockings and faced wearing ugly striped ones to church, she attempted to make herself sick by standing on an ice bank in the graveyard; when that failed, she went to service bare-legged, leading to widespread local gossip that she ultimately addressed by publishing an explanatory letter in the town paper. During a later club-mandated fast to punish themselves for another disruption, her sister Una fainted at church, sparking public criticism of their upbringing. Despite these misadventures, Faith and her siblings continued playing in Rainbow Valley, once mistaking a neighbor in the dark for a ghost and fleeing in panic. She eventually celebrated the news of her father's upcoming wedding to Rosemary West alongside her family.

label: Quote
value: Faith said: "I hope the girls are nice. I don’t like most of the girls round here. Even the nice ones are poky. But the Blythe twins look jolly. I thought twins always looked alike, but they don’t. I think the red-haired one is the nicest."

label: Quote
value: Faith said: “I’ve heard of Mrs. Ford,” broke in Faith. “Bertie Shakespeare Drew told me about her. She was married fourteen years to a dead man and then he came to life.”

label: Quote
value: Faith said: “Oh, it’s got to go on now,” cried Faith. “It’s a matter of honour. Don’t you dare tell anyone, Una. If you do I’ll never tell you secrets again!”

label: Quote
value: Faith said: "I love birds. Only—would Aunt Martha’s cat eat it? It’s so tragic to have your pets eaten. I don’t think I could endure it a second time."

label: Quote
value: Faith said: "Just as nice as Mrs. Blythe—but different. I felt as if I wanted to hug her. She did hug me—such a nice, velvety hug. And she called me ‘dearest.’ It thrilled me. I could tell her anything."

label: History
value: The First Mate is an orange cat.
unit: The First Mate was an orange cat who was rescued nine years earlier by Captain Jim after being found starving in a tree, entangled by his ribbon collar. Residing at the Four Winds Point lighthouse, he spent his time keeping Captain Jim company and entertaining visiting guests like Anne, Gilbert, and Leslie during their frequent social gatherings and New Year's celebrations. As Captain Jim neared the end of his life, he poignantly asked Anne to take care of the First Mate after his impending death. Following Captain Jim's peaceful passing in his sleep, the First Mate lost his long-time companion at the lighthouse.

label: History
value: Gilbert Blythe grows up in Avonlea
unit: Gilbert Blythe grows up in Avonlea after spending three years in Alberta for his father's health. Returning to school, he attempts to make peace with Anne Shirley after pulling her hair, but she smashes a slate over his head and refuses to speak to him for years. Despite her stony silence, Gilbert enters an intense academic rivalry with her, ultimately tying with her for first place on the Island on the Queen's Academy entrance examinations. After completing their studies at Queen's, Gilbert wins the class medal, but he selflessly surrenders his appointed teaching position in Avonlea so Anne can stay near Green Gables. This generous act leads to their long-awaited reconciliation, and the two become close friends while working together to found the Village Improvement Society. As they grow older and attend Redmond College together, Gilbert's feelings turn romantic, but Anne rejects his initial marriage proposal, leaving him heartbroken. Distancing himself, he is briefly rumored to be involved with Christine Stuart, but after surviving a life-threatening battle with typhoid fever, he proposes to Anne a second time and earns her eager acceptance. Following their wedding in the Green Gables orchard, Gilbert and Anne move to Four Winds Harbor, where he begins his medical practice and they bond with local neighbors like Captain Jim and Leslie Moore. After enduring the tragic loss of their firstborn infant daughter, Joyce, Gilbert and Anne later welcome a healthy son named James Matthew. Following Captain Jim's peaceful death, Gilbert proposes purchasing the larger Morgan place in Glen St. Mary to accommodate their expanding family and medical practice. Settled in their new home at Ingleside, Gilbert continues his career as a dedicated local physician, attending to the community and reviving young Una Meredith when she faints during a church service.

label: Quote
value: Gilbert Blythe said: "Well, I must run up to MacPhersons’. Moody Spurgeon came home from Queen’s today for Sunday and he was to bring me out a book Professor Boyd is lending me."

label: Quote
value: Gilbert Blythe said: "You’re just tired, Anne. Come, forget it all and take a walk with me—a ramble back through the woods beyond the marsh. There should be something there I want to show you."

label: Quote
value: Gilbert Blythe said: "No. I only know it should be, from something I saw there in spring. Come on. We’ll pretend we are two children again and we’ll go the way of the wind."

label: Quote
value: Gilbert Blythe said: "Here’s a fallen tree with a cushion of moss. Sit down, Anne—it will serve for a woodland throne. I’ll climb for some apples. They all grow high—the tree had to reach up to the sunlight."

label: Quote
value: Gilbert Blythe said: "I persist in dreaming it, although it has often seemed to me that it could never come true. I dream of a home with a hearth-fire in it, a cat and dog, the footsteps of friends—and you!"

label: Personality
value: Harrison is a crusty old pipe-smoker.
unit: A crusty, crabbed, and lonesome old pipe-smoker, Harrison is known for an outspoken nature that he prides himself on, making him hard to please. Outwardly sympathetic and kind, he nevertheless dislikes being pitied and holds a prejudice against marriage. Though usually unconcerned with his appearance, he makes a point to wear a white collar during business deals so that looking prosperous deters others from trying to cheat him.

label: History
value: Mr. Harrison was in Scottsford, New Brunswick before settling in Avonlea
unit: Before settling in Avonlea, Mr. Harrison was an old bachelor who had lived in Scottsford, New Brunswick, having delayed marriage for a long time. His initial encounter with Anne Shirley was a fiery confrontation when he angrily accused her of letting her cow into his oat field. Shortly thereafter, Anne accidentally sold Mr. Harrison's Jersey cow, but he took her mistake good-naturedly, accepted her cow in exchange, and invited her for tea. Despite his skepticism regarding her teaching methods and his refusal to donate to her Village Improvement Society, the two forged a friendly acquaintance. During a devastating hailstorm in Avonlea, Mr. Harrison's parrot was killed. He eventually revealed to Anne that he and his wife, Emily, had previously separated over his parrot and housecleaning habits; the couple subsequently reconciled, and Emily returned to Avonlea. Shortly thereafter, Anne accidentally sold Mr. Harrison's Jersey cow, but he took her mistake good-naturedly, accepted her cow in exchange, and invited her for tea. label: Quote
value: Harrison said: “Who? Mrs. Lynde? Don’t you tell me I’m like that old gossip,” said Mr. Harrison irritably. “I’m not . . . not a bit. What have you got in that box?”

label: Quote
value: Harrison said: "I don’t, that’s a fact, and I’m mighty fond of it, too. I’m much obliged to you. It looks good on top. I hope it’s good all the way through."

label: Quote
value: Harrison said: "Well, I’ll tell you what, miss, you must help me eat it. I’ll put the kettle on and we’ll have a cup of tea. How will that do?"

label: Quote
value: Harrison said: "I see you haven’t much confidence in my ability to make tea. You’re wrong . . . I can brew up as good a jorum of tea as you ever drank. But go ahead yourself. Fortunately it rained last Sunday, so there’s plenty of clean dishes."

label: Quote
value: Harrison said: “I’m a crusty, lonesome, crabbed old chap,” he said aloud, “but there’s something about that little girl makes me feel young again . . . and it’s such a pleasant sensation I’d like to have it repeated once in a while.”

He was severely mistreated by them, enduring beatings and starvation that left him suffering from epileptic fits and growing up simple-minded. After his death, a ghost story spread among the local children claiming that his spirit haunted the nearby Bailey garden, which frightened them enough to avoid the area at night.

label: History
value: Jane Andrews grew up in Avonlea
unit: Jane Andrews grew up in Avonlea as a classmate and friend of Anne Shirley. During her schooldays, she joined the local "Story Club" organized by Anne to cultivate their imaginations and write romantic tales. As a young woman pursuing education, she eventually went into teaching. In addition to her own pursuits, she acted as an intermediary for her family, once making a formal marriage proposal on behalf of her shy brother Billy to Anne, which Anne declined. Jane later married a wealthy man, becoming the wife of a millionaire, though her marriage remained a happy one. She eventually returned to visit Avonlea along with her mother and Mrs. Jasper Bell to inspect Anne's wedding trousseau prior to Anne's marriage.

In line with her conscientious disposition, she possesses notable skill in cooking.

label: History
value: Jane Andrews grew up as a peer of Anne Shirley.
unit: Jane Andrews grew up as a peer and schoolmate of Anne Shirley, joining Anne's newly formed story club alongside Ruby Gillis and other local youth. She pursued her education with her friends, joining the Queen's Academy preparation class, passing the entrance examination, and attending Queen's alongside Anne and Ruby. After completing her education, Jane worked as a teacher at the Avonlea school. Prior to resigning from her teaching position with plans to move West, Jane took part in social gatherings with her friends, including a spring birthday outing into the woods and pastures to discover Hester Gray's garden. During a Village Improvement Society effort, Jane joined Anne and Diana in attempting to persuade Judson Parker not to rent his fences for commercial advertisements. During an overnight visit with Anne, Jane acted as a proxy to propose marriage on behalf of her shy brother Billy; when Anne declined the proposal, Jane accepted the refusal coolly, noting that her brother would likely pursue another woman instead. Jane eventually went on to marry a millionaire, traveling to Europe for her honeymoon.

label: History
value: Miss Janet Sweet was a resident of Valley Road.
unit: Miss Janet Sweet was a resident of Valley Road who lived at Wayside, where she took in Anne Shirley as a boarder during Anne's time as a local schoolteacher. For twenty years, Janet was courted by her neighbor John Douglas, though he never proposed; on her fortieth birthday, she broke down in tears over the situation and briefly snubbed John following Anne's advice to stand up for herself. After John's overbearing mother passed away, John revealed that a secret oath to his late mother had prevented him from marrying, and he finally proposed to Janet.

label: Quote
value: Janet said: "Oh, she does. She’s told me time and again that she’d love to see John settled before her time comes. She’s always giving him hints—you heard her yourself the other day. I thought I’d ha’ gone through the floor."

label: Quote
value: Janet said: "You see, Anne, I’ve always been awful fond of John. He might just as well keep coming as not, for there was never anybody else I’d want, so it didn’t matter."

label: Quote
value: Janet said: "No, I guess not. I was afraid to try, anyway, for fear he’d think I meant it and just go. I suppose I’m a poor-spirited creature, but that is how I feel. And I can’t help it."

label: Quote
value: Janet said: "I know the road home pretty well alone. I ought to, seeing I’ve been traveling it for forty years. So you needn’t trouble yourself, Mr. Douglas."

label: Quote
value: Janet said: "Oh, I’m just as glad you did. When I saw John Douglas making off down that road I just felt as if every little bit of joy and happiness that was left in my life was going with him. It was an awful feeling."

Janet introduces Anne to local gatherings, such as a prayer meeting, and confides in her about her deeply troubled personal life, including her forty-year birthday distress over her stagnant courtship with John Douglas. Anne offers Janet advice to stand up for herself and later helps resolve the misunderstandings surrounding John's delay, while the two also share lighthearted moments like laughing together over unwanted suitors.

value: Jem said: “I’ve done my part frying the trout,” protested Jem, who hated saying grace. “Let Walter say it. He likes saying grace. And cut it short, too, Walt. I’m starving.”

label: History
value: Jerry Meredith is a child.
unit: Jerry Meredith is one of the motherless children of the new Presbyterian minister, Mr. Meredith. Growing up at the manse, he forms a tight-knit friendship with the Blythe children, frequently spending time with his siblings and neighbors sharing stories and trout in Rainbow Valley. Alongside his siblings Faith, Una, and Carl, Jerry takes in a runaway girl named Mary Vance, giving her shelter in their garret before she is eventually adopted by Miss Cornelia. During a period when his father is away and his aunt is bedridden, Jerry helps his family manage the household, and later, he joins his siblings in forming the Good-Conduct Club to police their own behavior and protect their father's public reputation.

value: Jerry said: "We’ll have a session of the Club first thing tomorrow and decide how we’ll do it. I never saw father so cut up. But I wish to goodness the Methodists would stick to one night for their prayer meeting and not wander all over the week."

value: Jerry said: "Of course it’s hard—but that’s the punishment of it. I could eat a graven image this very minute, but am I complaining? Let’s think of something else. We’ve just got to rise above our stomachs."

label: Quote
value: Jerry said: "is that Carl was the most to blame. He bolted first, as I understand it. Besides, he was a boy, so he should have stood his ground to protect you girls, whatever the danger was. You know that, Carl, don’t you?"

value: Jerry said: "If you’ll vote for Amesbury, Parker . . . well, I’ve a note for that pair of harrows you’ve got in the spring. I suppose you wouldn’t object to having it back, eh?"

value: Jerry said: "I’d like that corner near the road, I guess. I could hear the teams going past and the people talking."

value: John Douglas courted Janet.

Shortly after his mother passed away, John visited Wayside and proposed to Janet, revealing that his late mother had forced him to swear a secret oath never to marry while she was still alive.

label: History
value: In his youth, John Meredith went by the name Jack.
unit: In his youth, John Meredith went by the name Jack and later loved his wife, Cecelia, so deeply that he believed he could never care for another woman after her death. While serving as minister in Glen St. Mary, he frequently became engrossed in his reading and theology, leading him to neglect his parish duties and oversight of his children. Shaken by accusations of neglect from Mrs. Alec Davis, he admitted his shortcomings as a father and sought advice on parenting. Over time, he fell deeply in love with Rosemary West and proposed to her, but she reluctantly sent him a cold refusal due to a secret childhood vow made with her sister. Heartbroken, John resolved to be a better father to his children even though he believed he could never marry anyone other than Rosemary, later finding himself unable to strictly discipline his son Carl.

Shaken by accusations of neglect from Mrs. Alec Davis, he admitted his shortcomings as a father and sought advice on parenting. Over time, he fell deeply in love with Rosemary West and proposed to her, but she reluctantly sent him a cold refusal due to a secret childhood vow made with her sister. Heartbroken, John resolved to be a better father to his children even though he believed he could never marry anyone other than Rosemary, later finding himself unable to strictly discipline his son Carl.

He was subject to periodic trances, a trait he shared with a great-great-grandmother who had been burned as a witch, and which he viewed as either a gift or a curse. Decades later, his grandson Owen Ford traveled to the region, drawn by his connection to John Selwyn.

unit: Jonas Blake was a theological student who spent a summer at Cousin Emily's boardinghouse at Prospect Point, having resisted becoming a minister for a long time before pursuing his studies. During his time there, he met Philippa Gordon, who initially found him funny and ugly. However, after delivering a deeply moving sermon, he earned her profound admiration and caused her to nervously realize that she might be falling in love with him.

Upon arrival, he was repeatedly attacked by the resident stray cat, Rusty, though the two eventually resolved their conflicts and became close friends.

label: History
value: Josie Pye was the last of her family to attend the Avonlea school.
unit: Josie Pye was the last of her family to attend the Avonlea school, where she had once earned first prize for knitted lace at the exhibition. During a party at Diana Barry's house, she challenged Anne Shirley to walk the ridgepole of Mr. Barry's roof, an act that resulted in Anne falling and breaking her ankle. Later, Josie was among the group of Avonlea students who attended the local school under Miss Stacy's guidance and eventually pursued higher education at Queen's Academy.

label: History
value: Before her marriage, Lavendar Lewis lived at Echo Lodge.
unit: Before her marriage, Lavendar Lewis lived at Echo Lodge with her young servant, Charlotta the Fourth, named by her father after lavender because he was so fond of the scent. After accidentally wandering onto her property, Anne Shirley introduced Lavendar to Paul Irving, leading Lavendar to share her quiet sadness and reveal her past broken engagement with Paul's father, Stephen Irving. Anne subsequently helped arrange a reunion between Lavendar and Stephen, leading to their reconciliation, engagement, and a garden wedding at Echo Lodge. Following her marriage, Echo Lodge was closed, though Lavendar eventually hosted visits from Anne and questioned her regarding her complicated relationship with Gilbert Blythe.

label: Quote
value: Lavendar Lewis said: "But oh, won’t you stay and have tea with me? Please, do. Mr. Kimball’s will have tea over before you get there. And Charlotta the Fourth and I will be so glad to have you."

label: Quote
value: Lavendar Lewis said: "It gave me a shock to hear about Stephen’s son that first day you were here, Anne. I’ve never been able to mention him to you since, but I’ve wanted to know all about him. What sort of a boy is he?"

label: Quote
value: Lavendar Lewis said: "Oh, I’m not so old as I thought . . . and I don’t need a single blue pill! Girls, when you come back with your strawberries we’ll have tea out here under the silver poplar. I’ll have it all ready for you with home-grown cream."

label: Quote
value: Lavendar Lewis said: "About your age I think. He ought to be older because I dreamed him long before you were born. But I’ll never let him get any older than eleven or twelve; because if I did some day he might grow up altogether and then I’d lose him."

label: Quote
value: Lavendar Lewis said: "I’m wholesomely ashamed to think that a new dress . . . even it is a forget-me-not organdy . . . should exhilarate me so, when a good conscience and an extra contribution to Foreign Missions couldn’t do it."

label: History
value: Leslie Moore faced early tragedy
unit: Leslie Moore faced early tragedy, discovering her father after he committed suicide at age fourteen, and at sixteen she was coerced into marrying Dick Moore to save her mother's farm from foreclosure. A year later, her mother passed away. After meeting her neighbor Anne Blythe on the shore of Four Winds Harbor, Leslie formed a close, lasting friendship with her, eventually overcoming initial bitterness and confessing her painful past and complex feelings during a heart-to-heart in the garden. She hosted writer Owen Ford as a summer boarder, and during his stay, she secretly fell in love with him while maintaining her devotion to her household duties. When Gilbert Blythe proposed a brain operation that might restore Dick's memory, Leslie decided to proceed with the procedure and traveled to Montreal. The operation revealed that her dependent husband was actually Dick's cousin George Moore, freeing her from her long burden when George's sister took him home. Returning to Four Winds, Leslie stayed with Anne to help around the house and reconnected with Owen Ford upon his return. They confessed their mutual love in the garden and became engaged. After receiving Captain Jim's blessing shortly before his peaceful death, Leslie looked forward to a future with Owen, who arranged to purchase Anne and Gilbert's home as a summer residence.

unit: Leslie Moore faced early tragedy, discovering her father after he committed suicide at age fourteen, and at sixteen she was coerced into marrying Dick Moore to save her mother's farm from foreclosure. A year later, her mother passed away. After meeting her neighbor Anne Blythe on the shore of Four Winds Harbor, Leslie formed a close, lasting friendship with her, eventually overcoming initial bitterness and confessing her painful past and complex feelings during a heart-to-heart in the garden. She hosted writer Owen Ford as a summer boarder, and during his stay, she secretly fell in love with him while maintaining her devotion to her household duties. When Gilbert Blythe proposed a brain operation that might restore Dick's memory, Leslie decided to proceed with the procedure and traveled to Montreal. The operation revealed that her dependent husband was actually Dick's cousin George Moore, freeing her from her long burden when George's sister took him home. Returning to Four Winds, Leslie stayed with Anne to help around the house and reconnected with Owen Ford upon his return. They confessed their mutual love in the garden and became engaged. After receiving Captain Jim's blessing shortly before his peaceful death, Leslie looked forward to a future with Owen, who arranged to purchase Anne and Gilbert's home as a summer residence.

label: Quote
value: Leslie Moore said: "I knew who YOU were, although I had never seen either of you before. I had heard of the new doctor and his bride who were coming to live in Miss Russell’s little house. I—I hated you that very moment, Anne."

label: Quote
value: Leslie Moore said: "She is mistaken—or prejudiced. I think my figure IS better—mother was slight and bent by hard work—but she had the face of an angel. I used just to look up at her in worship. We all worshipped her,—father and Kenneth and I."

label: Quote
value: Leslie Moore said: “Kenneth was my brother,” went on Leslie. “Oh, I can’t tell you how I loved him. And he was cruelly killed. Do you know how?”

label: Quote
value: Leslie Moore said: "Anne, I saw his little face as the wheel went over him. He fell on his back. Anne—Anne—I can see it now. I shall always see it. Anne, all I ask of heaven is that that recollection shall be blotted out of my memory. O my God!"

label: Quote
value: Leslie Moore said: "I can’t tell you—don’t ask me. I wouldn’t mind your knowing—I wish you did know—but I can’t tell you—I can’t tell anyone. I’ve been such a fool, Anne—and oh, it hurts so terribly to be a fool. There’s nothing so painful in the world."

value: Mrs. Lynde was married at the age of eighteen.

When Anne Shirley accidentally caused trouble by jumping onto Aunt Josephine Barry during a game, Mrs. Lynde discussed the error with Anne before the girl set out to apologize. She later commended Anne's personal growth to Marilla at the end of a school term. Recognizing Anne's plain wardrobe, Mrs. Lynde secretly agreed to sew a stylish brown dress with puffed sleeves for Matthew Cuthbert to give Anne as a Christmas present. label: Personality
value: Marilla Cuthbert is a sober, middle-aged woman.
unit: A sober, middle-aged woman, she is known for her sensible, self-contained demeanor and rigid conscience. Characterized as strict, stern, and repressed, she generally views life through prose, detests cats, and rarely permits herself to display excitement or deep emotion. Despite her unsympathetic and critical tendencies, she is deeply determined and occasionally yields to subtle affection or sarcasm following a moment of self-betrayal. She has felt a duty to drill Anne into a tranquil uniformity of disposition, though she also worries over her and suffers from frequent headaches. Celebrated in Avonlea for making three-year-old homemade currant wine, she is also skilled at crafting round braided mats. Her quiet hopes were realized when she experienced profound happiness upon learning that Anne was going to marry Gilbert Blythe.

value: Marilla Cuthbert and her brother Matthew decided to adopt an orphan boy from Nova Scotia.
unit: Marilla Cuthbert and her brother Matthew decided to adopt an orphan boy from Nova Scotia to help with farm work at Green Gables, but a mix-up resulted in a young girl named Anne Shirley arriving instead. Although initially shocked and intent on returning her, Marilla grew pity for Anne's past, agreed to let her stay, and took on the task of raising and educating her. Despite early friction over Anne's dramatic behavior—including an incident where Anne accidentally gave currant wine to a friend and another where Marilla wrongly accused Anne of losing her inherited amethyst brooch—Marilla developed a deep affection for the child. When Matthew suddenly passed away and Marilla faced losing her failing eyesight, she considered selling Green Gables, but Anne gave up her college scholarship to stay home and teach locally. Marilla later agreed to take in her dying cousin's orphaned twins, Davy and Dora Keith, and took on her long-time neighbor Rachel Lynde as a housemate so Anne could attend Redmond College. She hosted Anne's wedding to Gilbert Blythe at Green Gables and traveled to Four Winds Harbor to visit the newlyweds, supporting Anne through both the tragic loss of her firstborn infant and the joyful birth of her son.

She hosted Anne's wedding to Gilbert Blythe at Green Gables and traveled to Four Winds Harbor to visit the newlyweds, supporting Anne through both the tragic loss of her firstborn infant and the joyful birth of her son.

value: Marilla Cuthbert said: "It’s five miles; and as you’re evidently bent on talking you might as well talk to some purpose by telling me what you know about yourself."

label: History
value: Marshall was a noted dancer in his youth.
unit: In his youth, Marshall was a noted dancer who was well acquainted with Miss Cornelia when he lived over-harbour. He famously made a public vow not to shave his face or cut his hair until the Liberal political party came to power, a strangely bearded appearance he maintained for years until the Liberals finally won a federal election and he shaved. Now married to Miss Cornelia, Marshall was consulted by his wife when Una Meredith asked her to adopt the orphaned Mary Vance. He agreed to the proposal, allowing Miss Cornelia to officially take Mary into their home.

label: History
value: Mary Vance ran away from a traumatic past.
unit: After running away from a traumatic past, the starved waif Mary Vance was found hiding in an old barn by the Meredith children, who fed her at the manse and introduced her to the local youth. She settled into the manse while taking on house chores, but feared being sent to an orphan asylum after Miss Cornelia confronted Mr. Meredith about her background. Una Meredith bravely asked Miss Cornelia to adopt Mary, and after consulting her husband, Miss Cornelia agreed to take the girl into her home. Living with Miss Cornelia, Mary proudly showed off new winter clothes to her friends in Rainbow Valley, though she frequently unsettled the other children by relaying local church gossip, telling frightening ghost stories, and sharing horror tales about stepmothers.

unit: After running away from a traumatic past, the starved waif Mary Vance was found hiding in an old barn by the Meredith children, who fed her at the manse and introduced her to the local youth. She settled into the manse while taking on house chores, but feared being sent to an orphan asylum after Miss Cornelia confronted Mr. Meredith about her background. Una Meredith bravely asked Miss Cornelia to adopt Mary, and after consulting her husband, Miss Cornelia agreed to take the girl into her home. Living with Miss Cornelia, Mary proudly showed off new winter clothes to her friends in Rainbow Valley, though she frequently unsettled the other children by relaying local church gossip, telling frightening ghost stories, and sharing horror tales about stepmothers.

label: Quote
value: Mary Vance said: "You think you’re something, don’t you, all dressed up like a doll! Look at me. My dress is all rags and I don’t care! I’d rather be ragged than a doll baby. Go home and tell them to put you in a glass case. Look at me—look at me—look at me!"

label: Quote
value: Mary Vance said: "If I ever find myself in a place where I ain’t licked I’ll think it’s heaven all right. No fear of me telling lies then. I ain’t fond of telling ‘em—I’d ruther not, if it comes to that."

label: Quote
value: Mary Vance said: "Give me Daniel. I’d rusher have it ‘cause I’m partial to lions. Only I wish they’d et Daniel up. It would have been more exciting."

label: Quote
value: Mary Vance said: "But it won’t be as easy for me to be good—inside, I mean, as well as outside—as it is for you. You hadn’t such scalawags of relations as I had."

label: Quote
value: Mary Vance said: "I never heard of any. My grandfather had money, but they say he was a rascal. No, I’ll just have to start out on my own hook and do the best I can."

label: Quote
value: Mary said: "Oh, I just got to thinking of things when I was here alone. I thought of having to go back to Mrs. Wiley—and of being licked for running away—and—and—and of going to hell for telling lies. It all worried me something scandalous."

label: Quote
value: Mary said: "I never thought of asking for anything in particular though. Nobody in this world ever bothered themselves about me so I didn’t s’pose God would. He might take more trouble for you, seeing you’re a minister’s daughter."

label: Quote
value: Mary said: “Well, as to this God-matter,” said Mary stubbornly, “since you and I can’t settle it, there ain’t no use in talking more about it until we’ve a chanct to find out the rights of it. I’ll do the best I can alone till then.”

label: Quote
value: Mary said: “I only wanted to warn you,” said Mary, rather repentantly. “Of course, your father’s so absent-minded he mightn’t happen to think of getting married again. But it’s better to be prepared.”

label: Quote
value: Mary said: "It was just awful of you. I wouldn’t have done such a thing for the world, and I weren’t brought up in a manse—weren’t brought up anywhere—just come up."

label: History
value: Matthew Cuthbert was raised by a shy, silent father.
unit: Matthew Cuthbert was raised by a shy, silent father who built a home far away from other people, and Matthew grew up to be the first person to offer love and sympathy to Anne Shirley's starved childhood. When he went to the station expecting to pick up an orphan boy to help on the farm, he was met instead by Anne and decided to bring her to Green Gables to let his sister Marilla handle the mistake. Matthew quietly advocated for keeping Anne and gave her simple delights, such as visiting her room to gently persuade her to apologize to Mrs. Lynde so she could stay, and gifting her a package of chocolate sweets. After Anne completed her studies at Queen's Academy, Matthew spent a tender final evening with her before dying suddenly from the shock of reading about the Abbey Bank failure.

Matthew quietly advocated for keeping Anne and gave her simple delights, such as visiting her room to gently persuade her to apologize to Mrs. Lynde so she could stay, and gifting her a package of chocolate sweets. After Anne completed her studies at Queen's Academy, Matthew spent a tender final evening with her before dying suddenly from the shock of reading about the Abbey Bank failure.

label: History
value: Matthew Cuthbert lived at Green Gables.
unit: Matthew Cuthbert lived at Green Gables, having grown up before the property's main house was built and wearing a soft brown beard since age twenty. Though so shy that local boys could not easily get acquainted with him, he drove to collect an orphan to bring home, dreading the moment the young girl, Anne, learned she had been brought by mistake instead of a boy. Matthew persistently advocated for keeping Anne, leaving Marilla to decide, and cheered when Marilla agreed to let her stay and properly educate her. Throughout Anne's childhood, Matthew warmly supported her, spending quiet evenings studying with her and encouraging her enthusiasm for a school concert despite Marilla's skepticism. Noticing Anne dressed more plainly than her peers, he overcame his shyness to procure a stylish brown dress with puffed sleeves as a Christmas gift for her. He continued to offer gentle guidance, joining a tea party with the minister and advising Anne not to give up on romance after a boating accident. Matthew proudly celebrated Anne's success when she tied for first place on the Island's entrance examinations and helped her prepare to attend Queen's Academy. Years later, after Anne married, she named her firstborn son James Matthew in honor of him.

value: Nan Blythe enjoyed spending time with her siblings in Rainbow Valley.
unit: Nan Blythe enjoyed spending time with her siblings in Rainbow Valley, where they formed a strong friendship with the Meredith children over a shared meal of freshly caught trout. When Mary Vance's former guardian passed away, Nan was the one who brought the shocking news to Mary and the gathered children in Rainbow Valley. She also fiercely defended her friend Faith Meredith alongside her sister Di when Mary Vance criticized Faith over a church scandal. As time passed, Nan continued to gather with her family and friends in Rainbow Valley, joining them to read poems, talk about future dreams, and eventually celebrate her brother Jem's final evening before he left for Queen's Academy.

value: Norman Douglas said: "‘Evening, girl. Sit down again—sit down again. I want to have a talk with you. Bless the girl, what’s she looking at me like that for? I don’t want to eat you—I’ve had my supper. Sit down and be civil."

label: Quote
value: Norman Douglas said: "So you can, girl, if you use your ears. I only wanted you to be comfortable. You look so durned uncomfortable, standing there. Well, I’ll sit anyway."

label: Quote
value: Norman Douglas said: "Let’s have a reasonable, sensible, friendly chat. There’s something I want to ask you. Ellen says she won’t, so it’s up to me to do it."

label: Quote
value: Norman Douglas said: "Well, a bargain is a bargain. I reckon I can stand it twelve times a year. What a sensation it’ll make the first Sunday I go! And old Susan Baker says I’m going to hell, hey? Do you believe I’ll go there—come, now, do you?"

label: Quote
value: Norman Douglas said: "Listen to her. You can’t cuddle a rooster as you can a kitten. Who ever heard of petting a rooster? Better take little Tom. I want to find a good home for him."

label: History
value: Owen Ford is a newspaper man.
unit: Owen Ford, a newspaper man and short story writer who suffered a bad spell of typhoid, was ordered to the sea by his doctor to recover his health. Arriving at Four Winds, he arranged to board with Leslie Moore and reconnected with the area through his grandfather, John Selwyn, while aspiring to write a great novel. He met Captain Jim, became enthralled by the old man's life experiences, and spent the summer working intensely at the lighthouse to write a manuscript combining Captain Jim's life story with the tale of lost Margaret. During his stay, Owen fell deeply in love with Leslie, but he departed at the end of the summer in agony over leaving her bound to her tragic marriage. Unaware that Leslie secretly harbored feelings for him, he later learned that her circumstances had changed when her husband's true identity was revealed. Owen returned to Four Winds for a visit, attempted to reconnect with Leslie, and ultimately confessed his love to her in the garden. After Leslie reciprocated his feelings and they sealed their commitment, they celebrated their future together alongside their friends and Captain Jim shortly before the old man's death.

value: Owen Ford said: "Yes,—he’s mentally deficient, or something of the sort, isn’t he? But she said nothing about Mrs. Moore, and I supposed she’d be the usual hustling country housewife who takes in boarders to earn an honest penny."

value: Owen Ford said: "Oh, I won’t mind him. I don’t suppose I’ll be much in the house anyhow, except for meals. But what a shame it all is! Her life must be a hard one."

label: History
value: Paul Irving was born in the United States.
unit: Paul Irving was born in the United States, but three years after his mother passed away, he moved to Avonlea to live with his grandmother. He became a pupil of Anne Shirley and quickly stood out as her favorite student due to his bright, imaginative nature and his fondness for poetic stories. Outside of school, Paul shared his creative ideas through letters and verse, including written descriptions of imaginary friends who lived along the shore. His rich inner life made him a natural companion for Anne, who visited him at his home and accompanied him on walks to the Avonlea cemetery and Echo Lodge to visit Miss Lavendar. During these visits, Paul bonded deeply with Miss Lavendar over their shared imaginative spirit, unaware at first of her history with his father, Stephen Irving. When Stephen returned to Avonlea and reconciled with Miss Lavendar, Paul shared in the family's joy surrounding their eventual wedding. Over time, his own poetry gained public recognition and was published in magazines. As he grew older, he maintained his affection for his former teacher, attending Anne's wedding at Green Gables prior to her departure for Glen St. Mary.

During these visits, Paul bonded deeply with Miss Lavendar over their shared imaginative spirit, unaware at first of her history with his father, Stephen Irving. When Stephen returned to Avonlea and reconciled with Miss Lavendar, Paul shared in the family's joy surrounding their eventual wedding. Over time, his own poetry gained public recognition and was published in magazines. As he grew older, he maintained his affection for his former teacher, attending Anne's wedding at Green Gables prior to her departure for Glen St. Mary.

label: History
value: Philippa Gordon is a lively and wealthy student
unit: Philippa "Phil" Gordon, a lively and wealthy student from an exclusive family in Bolingbroke, Nova Scotia, first met Anne Shirley and Priscilla Grant while exploring Old St. John's Cemetery on their first day at Redmond College. The three quickly formed a close friendship, and after Anne and Priscilla arranged to rent a house called Patty's Place, Phil asked to join their household for the following school year. While living at Patty's Place, she frequently entertained various suitors, but her romantic path changed during a summer trip when she met Jonas Blake, a theological student. Deeply moved after hearing him preach, Phil fell in love with him and eventually accepted his proposal, prioritizing him over her other admirers. Throughout college, Phil remained a confidante to Anne, comforting and confronting her through various romantic dilemmas involving Gilbert Blythe and Roy Gardner. Following graduation, Phil married Jonas. Years later, she and her husband attended Anne's wedding at Green Gables, by which point Phil had become thin after having babies of her own.

value: Phil Gordon said: "Heaps. The boys like me awfully—they really do. But there were only two that mattered. The rest were all too young and too poor. I must marry a rich man, you know."

label: Quote
value: Phil Gordon said: "And let me come to see you. I want to be chummy with you. I’ve taken such a fancy to you both. And I haven’t quite disgusted you with my frivolity, have I?"

label: Quote
value: Phil Gordon said: "I’ll go, if I can walk with Priscilla and Charlie. That will be a bearable degree of gooseberry. That Gilbert of yours is a darling, Anne, but why does he go around so much with Goggle-eyes?"

label: Quote
value: Phil Gordon said: "I don’t want William’s Island especially, but I’m sure I couldn’t get it if I did. Look at that sentry on the summit of the fort, right beside the flag. Doesn’t he look as if he had stepped out of a romance?"

label: Quote
value: Phil Gordon said: "Look—in white letters, around the archway over the gate. ‘Patty’s Place.’ Isn’t that killing? Especially on this Avenue of Pinehursts and Elmwolds and Cedarcrofts? ‘Patty’s Place,’ if you please! I adore it."

value: Mr. Phillips was a teacher
unit: Mr. Phillips was a teacher known for frequently whipping his students while failing to maintain any order in his classroom. During his time at the school, he disciplined Anne Shirley by making her stand in front of the class after she broke a slate over Gilbert Blythe's head, and later forced her to sit next to Gilbert as a further punishment. He eventually departed from his role as the local schoolmaster, leaving Anne emotional about his leaving as the community prepared to welcome a new minister and subsequent changes.

label: History
value: Priscilla Grant attended Queen's Academy
unit: Priscilla Grant attended Queen's Academy with her close friend Anne Shirley. Following her schooling, she was hired to teach at Carmody school. Later, she served as a conduit for famous author Charlotte E. Morgan—who was Priscilla's aunt—arranging visits and bringing Mrs. Morgan to Green Gables to meet Anne. When Priscilla matriculated at Redmond College in Kingsport, she warmly greeted Anne at the train station and helped her adjust to university life. While strolling through Old St. John's Cemetery, Priscilla and Anne befriended fellow student Philippa Gordon. Seeking a new residence for their upcoming school year, Priscilla and Anne discovered that Patty's Place was available for rent and successfully secured the home alongside Stella Maynard and Aunt Jamesina. Over the course of their college years, Priscilla shared in the lively home life at Patty's Place, hosted summer visits in Avonlea, and ultimately completed her studies at Redmond through Convocation.

label: Personality
value: Rachel Lynde is remarkably capable.
unit: A remarkably capable and hardworking individual, she excels at managing both her own concerns and those of others around her. Recognized as a kind and clever soul, she displays a deeply gentle and skillful nursing ability, serving as a patient, tender, and unwearied caregiver to her sick husband. She is famously outspoken and prides herself on speaking her mind without fear or favor, though others view her as a critical, meddlesome gossip who does not spare people when enumerating their shortcomings. Compulsively strict and corrective, she enjoys being asked for advice and maintains strong opinions, including a prejudice against Americans, political enthusiasm, and a profound skepticism toward both higher education for women and fiction writing. Practical by nature, she spends the leisure of her old age knitting cotton-warp quilts.

label: History
value: Mrs. Rachel Lynde lived as a long-time neighbor to Marilla Cuthbert in Avonlea.
unit: Mrs. Rachel Lynde lived as a long-time neighbor to Marilla Cuthbert in Avonlea, having raised ten children, buried two, and knitted sixteen cotton warp quilts. Eight years prior to Anne Shirley's arrival, she and her husband mortgaged their farm to start their youngest boy in the west. When she first learned of Marilla's plan to adopt an orphan, Mrs. Rachel expressed strong disapproval and warned her of the risks involved. She later visited Green Gables and insulted Anne's appearance, which provoked an angry outburst from the young girl; however, she completely forgiven Anne after receiving a dramatic apology. Mrs. Rachel continued to offer practical counsel, such as advising Marilla to let Anne stay home from school until she cooled down after a punishment, and keeping the household informed of local news and gossip. Following the death of her husband Thomas, Mrs. Rachel moved into Green Gables to live with Marilla, allowing Anne to leave her teaching post and attend Redmond College. label: History
value: Rosemary West grew up in the Glen.
unit: Rosemary West grew up in the Glen, where her little brother died, she kept a pet hen, and she attended school with local boys. After her mother's death, she stayed closely at home with her sister Ellen, with whom she clasped hands over their mother's Bible to vow they would never marry and would always live together. Years later, Rosemary met the widowed minister John Meredith by a hidden spring in Rainbow Valley. Though Ellen warned her against romance, John visited their home, and Rosemary later comforted his daughter Faith, earning the family's deep affection. When John eventually proposed, Rosemary realized she loved him and asked for time to consider, but Ellen strictly refused to release her from her vow, forcing Rosemary to send John a cold rejection letter. Later, Norman Douglas approached Rosemary at the spring to ask her to release Ellen from her vow so they could marry, which Rosemary granted; however, Ellen then refused to marry Norman if Rosemary was left living alone. Deeply moved when John's young daughter Una selflessly visited her and begged her to marry her father, Rosemary comforted the child, agreed to the proposal, and wrote a letter asking John to meet her.

label: History
value: Royal Gardner was a handsome Redmond student.
unit: Royal Gardner was a handsome Redmond student who had previously left college and gone abroad for two years due to his mother's failing health. He met Anne Shirley during a sudden rainstorm, rescuing her with his umbrella and walking her home before sending her a dozen roses. After escorting Anne to a reception and introducing his mother and sisters to her, Roy took her to the harbor pavilion upon their college graduation and proposed. However, Anne realized she did not love him and refused his offer, leaving Roy deeply upset as they parted ways.

value: Roy Gardner said: "I feel as if I didn’t belong anywhere yet. I put in my Freshman and Sophomore years at Redmond two years ago. I’ve been in Europe ever since. Now I’ve come back to finish my Arts course."

label: History
value: Ruby Gillis grew up in Avonlea.
unit: Ruby Gillis grew up in Avonlea as a classmate of Anne Shirley, having famously charmed away all her warts with a magic pebble as a child. A member of Anne's childhood story club, Ruby declared early on that she intended to have many suitors when she grew up. She attended school alongside Anne, eventually progressing with her to Queen's Academy to train as a teacher. Following their time at Queen's, Ruby gained a reputation for lively social chatter and flirtatious behavior back in Avonlea. However, she later fell terminally ill with consumption. Though she initially hid her failing health behind a façade of gaiety, Ruby eventually confided her deep fear of dying and her desire to live during an emotional evening with Anne. Shortly after that conversation, Ruby passed away peacefully in her sleep, leaving her friends to mourn her loss.

Following their time at Queen's, Ruby gained a reputation for lively social chatter and flirtatious behavior back in Avonlea. However, she later fell terminally ill with consumption. Though she initially hid her failing health behind a façade of gaiety, Ruby eventually confided her deep fear of dying and her desire to live during an emotional evening with Anne. Shortly after that conversation, Ruby passed away peacefully in her sleep, leaving her friends to mourn her loss.
